title: The resurrection end-silence — how it was received

nodes.label: Mark 16:8 — the end-silence
nodes.reading: Each account ends on a silence; Mark breaks off abruptly with the women afraid and saying nothing. What happens after is unnarrated, later supplied, or left open — the meaty end-gap.
nodes.title: The resurrection end-silence (Mark 16:8 · the unnarrated after)

nodes.label: Lake · Historical Evidence
nodes.reading: Lake treats the women's silence as the deliberate, emphatic main point of Mark's ending, while allowing that a now-lost continuation likely explained how they eventually spoke.
nodes.quoted_span: the deliberate silence of the women at the beginning — which is the main point — is perfectly plain, for the statement is quite emphatic
nodes.title: The Historical Evidence for the Resurrection of Jesus C

nodes.label: Orr (1908)
nodes.reading: Orr acknowledges Mark breaks off at the women's flight in trembling, but insists Mark's Gospel nonetheless implied — no less than the others — that a report followed.
nodes.quoted_span: St. Mark breaks off with the women fleeing from the tomb in "trembling and astonishment" ; but there can be no reasonable doubt that his Gospel also, not less than the others, contemplated a report of t
nodes.title: The Resurrection of Jesus — James Orr (1908)

nodes.label: Gould · ICC Mark
nodes.reading: Gould normalizes the abrupt ending as consistent with Mark's habitual brevity at the gospel's margins — not strange, not requiring explanation, simply characteristic.
nodes.quoted_span: Mark gives merely the announcement of the resurrection to the women by the angels, and closes with this. This, instead of being strange, and requiring explanation, is quite in accordance with the character of Mark
nodes.title: A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Gospel acco

nodes.label: Allen · ICC Matthew
nodes.reading: Allen reads Mark's silence as naturally inviting a follow-up appearance; Matthew, uneasy with it, rewrites the women as speaking, then continues with the appearance — but unmotivated.
nodes.quoted_span: It is very natural that this should have been followed by an appearance to them of Christ dispelling their fear and repeating the angel's message. Mt. alters "and told no one," etc., into "ran to tell His disciples."
nodes.title: A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Gospel acco

nodes.label: Longer Ending (16:9–20)
nodes.reading: The most consequential reception act: a later hand SUPPLIED an ending — appearances + commission + ascension — precisely because Mark's abrupt 16:8 silence was felt as a gap that had to be closed.
nodes.title: The Longer-Ending redactor (Mark 16:9-20)

nodes.label: Shorter Ending
nodes.reading: A second, briefer supplied ending in some manuscripts — independent evidence that the 16:8 silence generated MULTIPLE closure-attempts, not one.
nodes.title: The Shorter-Ending tradition

nodes.label: Narrative criticism
nodes.reading: Reads 16:8 not as a defect or accident but as an INTENTIONAL narrative choice — the silence forces the reader to supply the continuation (the 'hermeneutic of secrecy'). NOT in our corpus (the narrative-critical register is a known coverage gap, IRR228) — added as attested/inferred.
nodes.title: Narrative criticism (Kermode / Rhoads-Michie)
